唐.note:
The Li family's Tang dynasty (618–907). Its capital was Chang'an (the Upper Capital, or Western Capital), with Luoyang as the Eastern Capital and Taiyuan as the Northern Capital; during the An Lushan Rebellion Emperor Suzong made Fengxiang the Western Capital and Chengdu the Southern Capital (757–760).
The main thread of the mid and late Tang: after the An Lushan Rebellion (755–763) the three Hebei fanzhen became autonomous and Tibet seized Hexi and Longyou; Emperor Dezong's attempt to curb the fanzhen set off the Jianzhong rebellions (781–786); Emperor Xianzong's "Yuanhe Restoration" (806–820) for a time brought every fanzhen to obey the court; from Emperor Muzong on, Hebei rebelled again, eunuchs dominated the court and the Niu–Li factions fought; in the Dazhong era Emperor Xuanzong recovered Hehuang (849–851).
Under Emperors Yizong and Xizong, Pang Xun, Wang Xianzhi and Huang Chao rose one after another, and in 880 Huang Chao entered Chang'an; from then on the court's orders did not reach beyond Guanzhong, while Zhu Quanzhong, Li Keyong, Li Maozhen, Yang Xingmi and others carved out territories of their own.
In Tianyou 4 (907) Emperor Ai abdicated in favor of Zhu Quanzhong, and the Tang came to an end.

燕·安史.note: In the 11th month of 755 An Lushan rose at Fanyang, ostensibly "to punish Yang Guozhong"; in the 1st month of 756 he proclaimed himself emperor of Great Yan at Luoyang, and in the 6th month he broke through Tong Pass and entered Chang'an. In the 1st month of 757 An Qingxu murdered his father; the same year the Tang army, with Uyghur troops, recovered the two capitals, and An Qingxu fell back to hold Xiangzhou (Ye). In 759 Shi Siming killed An Qingxu, proclaimed himself emperor of Great Yan in turn, and took Luoyang again; in 761 Shi Chaoyi murdered his father; in the 1st month of 763 Shi Chaoyi was defeated and hanged himself, and the An Lushan Rebellion ended after eight years.

吐蕃.note:
The plateau empire founded by the Pugyal dynasty of Yarlung, with its capital at Rasa (Lhasa). It was at its height from the late 8th to the early 9th century: it broke into Chang'an in 763, took all of Hexi and Longyou in 764–786, captured Beiting in 790, and thereafter held the southern route of the Four Garrisons of Anxi; its power reached the Long Mountains in the east, Nanzhao in the south and beyond the Pamirs in the west.
Trisong Detsen (755–797) promoted Buddhism; in 821–822 Tibet and Tang made the Treaty of Changqing, and in 823 the Tang–Tibet Treaty Pillar was set up in front of the Jokhang Temple in Lhasa. In 842 the tsenpo Langdarma was assassinated, the royal house split, and the empire broke up.

吐蕃诸部.note: After 842 the Tibetan Empire split, the royal line dividing into the Yongdan and Ousong branches, while local magnates and frontier generals (Lun Kongre, Shang Bibi and others) fought one another; the Tibetan population of Hexi, Longyou and Qinghai scattered into many tribes, known to history as the "Tibetan tribes". Of these, the Wamo and the Liugu tribes around Liangzhou and the tribes around Qingtang (Xining) later became, respectively, the Zhebu clan's regime at Xiliang Fu and the Gusiluo regime of Song times.

回鹘.note:
In 744 Guli Peiluo destroyed the Second Turkic Khaganate and founded the Uyghur Khaganate, with its royal camp at Ordu-Baliq on the Orkhon River (today's Kharbalgas, Mongolia). In 757 it sent troops to help Tang recover the two capitals, and for a long time afterwards it made marriage alliances with Tang and traded horses for silk. In 788 its Chinese name was changed to Huihu. In the 790s it fought Tibet for Beiting and Xizhou.
In 840 the Yenisei Kyrgyz sacked its royal camp and the khaganate collapsed; its people moved west in three branches: one into Hexi (the Ganzhou Uyghurs), one into the eastern Tian Shan (the Xizhou or Qocho Uyghurs), and one to the Karluks.

黠戛斯.note: A Turkic-speaking people on the Kem River (the upper Yenisei), the Jiankun of Han times and the ancestors of the Kyrgyz of the Ming and Qing. In 840 they destroyed the Uyghur Khaganate and for a time held the lands north of the Gobi, sending envoys to Tang to seek investiture (843). In the early 10th century their power fell back to the Yenisei basin, and the lands north of the Gobi passed to the Zubu (Tatar) tribes.

葛逻禄.note: A branch of the Western Turks, originally living southwest of the Altai Mountains. At the Battle of Talas in 751 they changed sides in the middle of the fighting, causing Gao Xianzhi's Tang army to be routed. After 766 they moved south to the area of Suyab and Talas and replaced the Türgesh as masters of Semirechye; in the 9th–10th centuries they and the Yaghma and other tribes formed the core of the Kara-Khanid Khanate.

突骑施.note: A branch of the Western Turks that dominated Semirechye (Suyab, Talas) in the early 8th century. After the death of Suluk Khagan in 738 it fell into civil war and its people dispersed; in the 750s–760s it was replaced by the Karluks.

南诏.note:
Founded after the Mengshe zhao united the six zhao around Erhai Lake (Tang invested Piluoge as Prince of Yunnan in 738), with its capital at Taihe City; in 779 it moved to Yangjumie City (the old town of Dali). It defeated Tang armies twice, in 751 and 754 (the Tianbao wars), and became a dependent of Tibet; in 794 Yimouxun made a treaty with the Tang envoy Cui Zuoshi at the Diancang Mountains, returning to Tang allegiance against Tibet.
In the 9th century, under Quanfengyou and Shilong, the kingdom was powerful: it attacked Chengdu in 829, crushed Pyu in 832, took Annan several times in 858–866, and besieged Chengdu in 869–870. In 902 the powerful minister Zheng Maisi usurped the throne, and Nanzhao came to an end.

大长和.note: In 902 Zheng Maisi, chief minister of Nanzhao, killed the Nanzhao king Shunhuazhen and founded the kingdom of Dachanghe. In 928 Yang Ganzhen, military governor of Jianchuan, made Zhao Shanzheng emperor and renamed the state Datianxing; in 929 Yang Ganzhen took the throne himself and renamed it Dayining. In 937 Duan Siping destroyed Dayining and founded the Dali Kingdom.

大理.note: In 937 Duan Siping, military governor of Tonghai, allied with the thirty-seven eastern tribes, destroyed Dayining and founded the Dali Kingdom, with its capital at Yangjumie City (the old town of Dali). It revered Buddhism; according to tradition, Emperor Taizu of Song drew the border along the Dadu River with a jade axe ("the Song waves the jade axe"). It was destroyed by the Mongols in 1253.

渤海.note: Founded in 698 by Dae Joyeong, a chief of the Sumo Mohe; it was first called Jin. In 713 Tang invested him as Commandery Prince of Bohai. It had five capitals, fifteen fu and sixty-two prefectures; its Supreme Capital, Longquan Fu (today's Bohai Town, Ning'an), was laid out on the model of Chang'an. In the 9th century, under Dae Insu and Dae Ijin, it was called "the flourishing land east of the sea". In 926 it was destroyed by the Khitan and turned into the Dongdan kingdom.

东丹.note: A dependent state set up by the Khitan after they destroyed Balhae in 926, with the crown prince Yelü Bei as Renhuang Wang (King of Men) and its capital at Huhan City (the Balhae Supreme Capital). In 928 its people were moved to Liaodong, with Dongping (Liaoyang) as the Southern Capital; in 930 Yelü Bei crossed the sea and went over to the Later Tang. Dongdan survived in name only, and its Central Secretariat was abolished in 982.

契丹.note:
Nomads of the Huang River (Xar Moron) and Tu River (Laoha River) basins; in the early Tang (648) they were held on a loose rein through the Songmo Area Command. In the period of the eight-tribe confederation under the Yaonian clan they repeatedly fought Tang, the Xi and the Uyghurs. In 907 Yelü Abaoji of the Yila tribe became khagan; he proclaimed himself emperor in 916, built Huangdu (the Supreme Capital, Linhuang Fu) in 918, campaigned west across the lands north of the Gobi in 924, and destroyed Balhae in 926.
In 936 the Khitan helped Shi Jingtang destroy the Later Tang, and in 938 they acquired the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun. In 947 Yelü Deguang entered Kaifeng, destroyed the Later Jin and renamed the state Great Liao. In 979 they routed the Song army at the Battle of the Gaoliang River.

奚.note: The Kumo Xi, living southwest of the Khitan (on the upper Laoha and Luan rivers today); Tang set up the Raole Area Command for them. With the Khitan they were known as "the two Fan", and they wavered between Tang and the Uyghurs. In the early 10th century they were conquered by Yelü Abaoji and absorbed into the Khitan state; the later Liao Central Capital, Dading Fu, was built on the site of the Xi king's camp.

室韦.note: Many tribes spread east and west of the Greater Khingan and along the Nen and Argun rivers, of the same origin as the Khitan. In Tang times they were divided into more than twenty tribes; among them the Mengwu Shiwei, who lived along the Wangjian River (the Argun), were the ancestors of the Mongols.

黑水靺鞨.note: The northernmost of the seven Mohe tribes, living along the Heishui (the Amur and the lower Songhua). Tang set up the Heishui Area Command in 726. When Balhae was strong they were largely under its control; from the 10th century they were called Jurchens.

女真.note: Descendants of the Heishui Mohe, known from the 10th century as the Jurchens (Nüzhen; also written Nüzhi to avoid the personal name of Emperor Xingzong of Liao). Those whom the Khitan moved south and entered in the household registers were called the Civilized Jurchens, those not registered the Wild Jurchens. In 1115 Wanyan Aguda founded the Jin.

阻卜.note: The tribes active north of the Gobi from the 10th century, called Tatars by the Song and Zubu by the Liao, including the later Keraites, Merkits and Tatars. From 924 they nominally submitted to the Khitan, rebelling and submitting by turns.

新罗.note: In 676 it unified the Korean peninsula south of the Taedong River, with its capital at Geumseong (today's Gyeongju). In 735 Tang formally recognized its possession of the land south of the Paegang (the Taedong River). At the end of the 9th century royal power declined and local magnates ("castle lords" and "generals") carved out territories of their own, opening the "Later Three Kingdoms" period; in 935 King Gyeongsun surrendered to Goryeo.

后百济.note: In 892 the Silla general Gyeon Hwon rose in arms and seized Mujinju (Gwangju); in 900 he proclaimed himself king at Wansanju (Jeonju), with the state name Baekje, known to history as Later Baekje. In 927 he broke into the Silla capital, Geumseong. It was destroyed by Goryeo in 936.

泰封.note: Gung Ye, a member of the Silla royal house, proclaimed himself king at Songak in 901 (with the state name Goryeo, known to history as Later Goguryeo); in 904 he renamed the state Majin, in 905 moved the capital to Cheorwon, and in 911 renamed it Taebong. In 918 his general Wang Geon staged a coup and founded Goryeo.

高丽.note: In 918 Wang Geon overthrew Gung Ye and founded Goryeo, settling the capital at Songak (Gaegyeong, today's Kaesong) in 919. Silla surrendered in 935, and in 936 Goryeo destroyed Later Baekje and unified the Korean peninsula. With Pyongyang as its Western Capital, Seogyeong, it extended its rule north to around the Cheongcheon River.

日本.note: From the end of the Nara period into the Heian period (the capital moved to Heian-kyō in 794). Embassies to Tang continued until 894, when Sugawara no Michizane proposed ending them. Tang and Silla merchants traveled between Dazaifu at Hakata and Mingzhou, Yangzhou and Chuzhou.

骠国.note: A city-state of the Pyu people, with its capital at Sri Ksetra (near today's Pyay). In 802 it sent musicians to Chang'an with a Nanzhao embassy to present their music, and Bai Juyi wrote the poem Piaoguo yue. It was crushed by Nanzhao in 832.

蒲甘.note: A kingdom founded by the Burmans on the middle Irrawaddy; by traditional reckoning its history begins with the building of the city of Pagan in 849. In the 11th century, under Anawrahta, it unified Burma.

文单.note: The northern part of Chenla after it split, "Land Chenla", which the Tang called the state of Wendan, roughly around today's Vientiane, Laos. In 753 a prince of Wendan led his followers to join the Tang campaign against Nanzhao, and in 771 it sent envoys to Tang.

环王.note: The kingdom of the Cham people, called Linyi in Han times, Huanwang after the Zhide era of Tang (756–758), and Zhancheng (Champa) from the late 9th century. From 875 its capital was Indrapura (today's Đồng Dương, Da Nang, Vietnam). It fought Annan and Chenla from time to time.

泥婆罗.note: The Licchavi dynasty of the Kathmandu Valley, a vassal of Tibet in the 7th–8th centuries; the Tang envoy Wang Xuance once borrowed troops from it.

于阗.note: An oasis kingdom on the southern rim of the Tarim Basin, ruled by the hereditary Viśa (Yuchi) royal house. Under Tang it was one of the Four Garrisons of Anxi (the Pisha Area Command); it fell to Tibet in the 790s and regained independence in the mid 9th century. Li Shengtian (Viśa Saṃbhava, r. 912–966) made marriage alliances with the Cao family of Shazhou and in 938 was invested by the Later Jin as "King of Great Treasure Khotan". In the late 10th century it fought a long war with the Kara-Khanid Khanate and was destroyed by the Kara-Khanids around 1006.

西州回鹘.note: After the Uyghur Khaganate collapsed in 840, Pang Tegin led his followers west to the area of Karasahr and Kucha in the eastern Tian Shan. In 866 Pugu Jun of the Beiting Uyghurs took Xizhou, Beiting and Luntai and made Qocho his capital: this was the Kingdom of Qocho (also called the Xizhou Uyghurs or the Tian Shan Uyghurs), with Beiting (Beshbaliq) as its summer capital.

高昌回鹘.note: In 866 Pugu Jun seized Xizhou (Qocho) and Beiting and founded the Kingdom of Qocho, wintering at Qocho and summering at Beiting; it ruled the eastern Tian Shan together with Karasahr and Kucha. Its people followed Manichaeism and Buddhism, and it left a wealth of murals and manuscripts (the Bezeklik Caves). It submitted to the Mongols in 1209.

甘州回鹘.note: Uyghurs who moved into Hexi after 840. At the end of the 9th century (c. 894) they set up their royal camp at Ganzhou, and they addressed the Central Plains courts as "maternal uncle". They controlled the middle of the Hexi Corridor and alternately fought and made peace with the Guiyi Jun at Shazhou. They were destroyed by Western Xia in 1028.

喀喇汗.note: A dynasty founded by the Karluk, Yaghma and other Turkic tribes in Semirechye and Kashgar (c. 840s–1212), with Balasagun and Kashgar as its two capitals. Satuq Bughra Khan converted to Islam c. 934, making it the first Turkic Muslim dynasty in Central Asia. From the late 10th century it waged a long "holy war" against Khotan.

归义军.note:
In 848 Zhang Yichao, of a powerful Shazhou family, led a rising that drove out the Tibetans, recovered Guazhou and Shazhou, and went on to take Ganzhou, Suzhou, Yizhou and other prefectures; in 851 he sent his elder brother Zhang Yitan to the court with the maps and registers of eleven prefectures, and Tang set up the Guiyi Jun at Shazhou with Zhang Yichao as military governor. Liangzhou was recovered in 861.
The Zhang line passed down to Zhang Chengfeng, who in 910 founded the "Golden Mountain Kingdom of the Western Han"; defeated by the Ganzhou Uyghurs in 911, it was reduced to the "Kingdom of Dunhuang". In 914 Cao Yijin replaced the Zhang family and restored the name Guiyi Jun, and the Cao family held Guazhou and Shazhou for generations, into the 11th century. Most of the manuscripts of the Dunhuang Library Cave date from this period.

凉州蕃部.note: After the Tibetan Empire collapsed, the Liangzhou area was controlled by the Wamo (slave tribes of the Tibetans who had risen in revolt) and the Liugu Tibetan tribes; in the late Tang and Five Dynasties a military governor of Liangzhou existed in name, but in practice it was a self-governing mix of Tibetans and Han Chinese. In the late 10th century the Zhebu clan led it, and the Song called it Xiliang Fu; it was taken by Western Xia in the early 1030s.

定难.note: Tuoba Sigong, chief of the Tuoba tribe of the Tanguts, helped Tang suppress Huang Chao; in 881–882 he was made military governor of Xiazhou (the Dingnan Jun), and in 883 he was granted the imperial surname Li for his services. His family held the four prefectures of Xiazhou, Suizhou, Yinzhou and Youzhou (later also Jingzhou) for generations. In the Five Dynasties it nominally obeyed the Central Plains courts but was in fact a hereditary, independent regime. In 982 Li Jipeng surrendered its lands to Song; his clansman Li Jiqian fled to resist Song, and Li Jiqian's grandson Li Yuanhao founded Western Xia in 1038.

定安国.note: A regime founded by Balhae survivors on the upper Yalu River (c. mid-10th century to the end of the 10th century), which sent envoys to Song twice, in 970 and 981. It was destroyed by Liao c. 986.

朱泚.note: In the 10th month of 783 the Jingyuan troops mutinied as they passed through Chang'an and acclaimed the Grand Commandant Zhu Ci, former military governor of Lulong; Zhu Ci proclaimed himself emperor of Great Qin and besieged Emperor Dezong at Fengtian, and in the 1st month of the next year renamed the state Han. In the 5th month of 784 Li Sheng recovered Chang'an; Zhu Ci fled west and was killed by his own officers on the way.

李怀光.note: Li Huaiguang, military governor of Shuofang, led his army to lift the siege of Fengtian, but fell out with the chief minister Lu Qi and with Bai Zhizhen; in the 2nd month of 784 he joined Zhu Ci in rebellion, and Emperor Dezong fled again, to Liangzhou. In the 8th month of 785 Ma Sui and Hun Jian besieged Hezhong, and Li Huaiguang hanged himself.

大楚.note: Li Xilie, military governor of Huaixi, was ordered to attack Li Na but instead colluded with four fanzhen; in 782 he styled himself Prince of Jianxing and Generalissimo of All Under Heaven. In the 12th month of 783 he took Bianzhou, and in the 1st month of 784 proclaimed himself emperor of a state called Great Chu. His repeated attacks on Chenzhou and Xiangcheng failed and he fell back to Caizhou; in 786 he was poisoned by his officer Chen Xianqi.

大齐.note: Huang Chao entered Chang'an in the 12th month of 880 and took the imperial throne in the Hanyuan Hall, with the state name Great Qi and the reign title Jintong. Unable to control anything beyond Guanzhong and with his supply lines cut, he was driven out of Chang'an in the 4th month of 883 by Li Keyong's Shatuo army and others, and in the 6th month of 884 he was defeated and died at Langhu Valley near Mount Tai.

罗平.note: Dong Chang, military governor of the Yisheng Jun (Zhedong), proclaimed himself emperor at Yuezhou in the 2nd month of 895, with the state name Great Yue Luoping. In 896 Qian Liu, acting on an imperial order, took Yuezhou; Dong Chang was killed, and all of Liangzhe passed to Qian Liu.

后梁.note: 907–923. Founded by Zhu Quanzhong (Zhu Wen, later renamed Zhu Huang) when he usurped the Tang throne, with its capital at Kaifeng (the Eastern Capital) and Luoyang as the Western Capital. It waged a long seesaw war with Li Cunxu of Hedong in Hebei and along the Yellow River: it was defeated twice by Jin, at the siege camp of Luzhou in 908 and at Baixiang in 911, and in 915 Weibo surrendered to Jin. In 923 Li Cunxu sent Li Siyuan in a surprise attack on Kaifeng; the last emperor, Zhu Youzhen, killed himself, and the Liang came to an end.

晋.note: 907–923. The Shatuo Li Keyong (d. 908) and his son Li Cunxu held Hedong; refusing to recognize the Liang calendar, they kept the Tang reign title Tianyou and kept the title Prince of Jin. In 908 Li Cunxu relieved the siege of Luzhou (at Sanchui Ridge), in 911 he crushed the Liang army at Baixiang, in 913 he destroyed Liu Shouguang's Yan, in 915 he gained Weibo, and in 923 he proclaimed himself emperor at Weizhou (the Later Tang).

燕·刘.note: Liu Rengong, military governor of Lulong, and his son Liu Shouguang. In 907 Liu Shouguang imprisoned his father and took his place, and in 911 he proclaimed himself emperor of Great Yan. In 913 the Jin general Zhou Dewei took Youzhou, and father and son were captured and killed.

岐.note: 887–924. Li Maozhen (born Song Wentong, granted the surname Li), military governor of Fengxiang, held Fengxiang, Longyou and Shannan West Circuit; at the end of the Tang he once seized Emperor Zhaozong, and in 902–903 he was besieged for a year by Zhu Quanzhong. After 907 he opened the court of the Prince of Qi, did not proclaim himself emperor, and kept the Tang calendar; his territory was gradually eaten away by the Former Shu and the Later Liang. In 924 he submitted to the Later Tang as a vassal and died soon after.

前蜀.note: 907–925. Wang Jian entered Chengdu in 891, annexed Dongchuan, Shannan West Circuit and the prefectures along the Yangtze Gorges, and in the 9th month of 907 proclaimed himself emperor of a state called Shu, with its capital at Chengdu. Wang Yan was dissolute, and in 925 the Later Tang sent Guo Chongtao against Shu, which fell in seventy days.

后唐.note: 923–936. Li Cunxu proclaimed himself emperor of a state called Tang at Weizhou in 923, destroyed the Liang the same year, and moved the capital to Luoyang; in 925 he destroyed the Former Shu. In the Xingjiao Gate incident of 926 Zhuangzong was killed and Li Siyuan (Mingzong) took the throne, a reign remembered as a time of modest prosperity. In 934 Meng Zhixiang proclaimed himself emperor in Shu; in 936 Shi Jingtang of Hedong brought Khitan troops south, and the last emperor, Li Congke, burned himself to death in Luoyang.

后晋.note: 936–947. Shi Jingtang founded the state with Khitan help, at the price of ceding the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun and calling himself the Khitan emperor's "son", and settled the capital at Kaifeng in 938. Emperor Chu (Shi Chonggui) called himself the Khitan emperor's grandson but refused to be his subject, which led to three wars: a great victory at Yangcheng (Baituanwei Village) in 945, Du Chongwei's surrender at Zhongdu Bridge in 946, and in the 1st month of 947 the Khitan entry into Kaifeng and the fall of the Later Jin.

后汉.note: 947–951. Liu Zhiyuan (a Shatuo), military governor of Hedong, proclaimed himself emperor at Taiyuan in the 2nd month of 947 and entered Kaifeng in the 6th month as the Liao army withdrew north. Liu Zhiyuan died in 948; the young and suspicious Emperor Yin, Liu Chengyou, put the senior ministers Yang Bin, Shi Hongzhao and others to death in 950 and planned to kill Guo Wei too; Guo Wei rose in arms, and Emperor Yin was killed.

后周.note: 951–960. Guo Wei proclaimed himself emperor in 951, with his capital at Kaifeng, and reformed the administration. In 954 his adopted son Chai Rong (Shizong) took the throne; after the Battle of Gaoping he reorganized the army, took Qinzhou and Fengzhou in the west, won the land north of the Yangtze in three campaigns against the Southern Tang, recovered Ying, Mo and the Three Passes in a northern campaign, restricted Buddhism and melted down bronze to cast coins, and enlarged the city of Kaifeng. Shizong died in 959, and in 960 Zhao Kuangyin replaced the Zhou in the Chenqiao mutiny.

北汉.note: 951–979. Liu Chong, younger brother of the Later Han founder and military governor of Hedong, proclaimed himself emperor at Taiyuan and depended on Liao, calling himself its "nephew emperor". With little land and a poor population, it had only twelve prefectures. In 979 Emperor Taizong of Song led a campaign in person; Liu Jiyuan came out to surrender, the city of Taiyuan was burned, and Bingzhou was moved to Tangming Town (today's urban Taiyuan).

宋.note: In 960 Zhao Kuangyin replaced the Zhou and founded the Song, with its capital at Kaifeng (the Eastern Capital). It followed a policy of "south first, then north": it took Jingnan and Hunan in 963, destroyed the Later Shu in 965, the Southern Han in 971 and the Southern Tang in 975; Wuyue and the Zhangzhou–Quanzhou regime surrendered their lands in 978, and the Northern Han was destroyed in 979. The same year Song marched north against Youzhou and was badly defeated at the Battle of the Gaoliang River; thereafter it faced Liao across the line of the Baigou River and Yanmen.

吴.note: 902–937. Yang Xingmi, military governor of Huainan, was made Prince of Wu by Tang in 902, with his capital at Guangling (Yangzhou). His great victory over Zhu Quanzhong at the Battle of Qingkou in 897 secured the independence of the Jianghuai region. After Yang Xingmi's death the powerful ministers Xu Wen and his adopted son Xu Zhigao controlled the government; Yang Longyan styled himself King of Wu in 919, and Yang Pu proclaimed himself emperor in 927. In 937 Xu Zhigao received the abdication of Wu and founded Qi (the Southern Tang).

南唐.note: 937–975. Xu Zhigao received the abdication of Wu and named the state Qi; in 939 he resumed the surname Li, took the name Li Bian and renamed the state Tang. Its capital was Jinling (Jiangning Fu). It guarded its borders and let its people rest, and its culture flourished (the lyrics of Li Jing and Li Yu, The Night Revels of Han Xizai). It destroyed Min in 945 and Chu in 951, but soon lost Hunan. Defeated by the Later Zhou in 956–958, it surrendered the fourteen prefectures north of the Yangtze and gave up the imperial title; in 961 it moved the capital to Nanchang (the Southern Capital), soon returning to Jinling. In 975 the Song army took Jinling and Li Yu came out to surrender.

吴越.note: 907–978. Qian Liu held Liangzhe and was made Prince of Wuyue by the Liang in 907, with his capital at Hangzhou (the Western Seat) and Yuezhou as the Eastern Seat. He built the stone seawall, carried out water-control works around Lake Tai, followed the calendar of the Central Plains courts, and "guarded the borders and kept the people at peace". Wuyue gained Fuzhou in 947. In 978 Qian Chu surrendered his lands to Song.

闽.note: 909–945. The brothers Wang Chao and Wang Shenzhi came into Fujian from Guangzhou (in today's Henan) and took Fuzhou in 893. In 909 Wang Shenzhi was made Prince of Min; he opened Gantang Harbor and attracted overseas merchants. In 933 Wang Yanjun proclaimed himself emperor and raised Fuzhou to Changle Fu. Members of the Wang family fought one another, and in 943 Wang Yanzheng proclaimed himself emperor of Yin at Jianzhou. In 945 the Southern Tang destroyed Min; at Fuzhou Li Renda surrendered to Wuyue (947), and Quanzhou and Zhangzhou passed to Liu Congxiao.

楚.note: 907–951. Ma Yin seized Tanzhou in 896 and was made Prince of Chu in 907, with his capital at Changsha. Chu grew rich on the tea trade and on casting lead and iron coins. Ma Yin's sons fought over the succession ("many colts fighting over one trough"), and in 951 the Southern Tang took advantage of the chaos to destroy Chu, while the Southern Han took its prefectures in Lingnan.

南汉.note: 917–971. Liu Yin held Guangzhou (the Qinghai Jun); the succession passed from brother to brother, and Liu Yan proclaimed himself emperor in 917 with the state name Great Yue, changed to Han the next year; the capital was Xingwang Fu (Guangzhou). Defeated by Ngô Quyền at the Battle of Bạch Đằng in 938, it lost Giao Châu. Its punishments were cruel and eunuchs dominated the government. In 971 the Song general Pan Mei broke into Guangzhou and Liu Chang came out to surrender.

南平.note: 907–963. Gao Jichang (later renamed Gao Jixing) became military governor of Jingnan under the Later Liang in 907 and was made Prince of Nanping by the Later Tang in 924. It held only the three prefectures of Jiangling, Guizhou and Xiazhou, at a crossroads between north and south; it declared itself a vassal of every neighbor to collect their gifts, earning the nickname "Gao the Scoundrel". In 963 the Song army asked for passage through Jingnan, and Gao Jichong surrendered his lands.

后蜀.note: 934–965. Meng Zhixiang became military governor of Xichuan in 925, annexed Dongchuan in 932, and proclaimed himself emperor in 934 with the state name Shu and his capital at Chengdu. Meng Chang reigned for thirty-one years; Shu was rich, and under him the anthology Among the Flowers was compiled and the Shu Stone Classics were carved. In the winter of 964 Song attacked Shu along two routes, and in the 1st month of 965 Meng Chang came out to surrender.

清源.note: After the Southern Tang destroyed Min, Liu Congxiao, an army officer at Quanzhou, seized Quanzhou and Zhangzhou in 947–949, and the Southern Tang made him military governor of the Qingyuan Jun. Liu Congxiao died in 962 and Chen Hongjin took power; in 964 Song made him military governor of the Pinghai Jun instead. In 978 Chen Hongjin surrendered Quanzhou and Zhangzhou to Song.

武平.note: After the Southern Tang destroyed Chu in 951, the Chu generals Liu Yan, Wang Kui and Zhou Xingfeng drove out the Southern Tang army in 952 and held Hunan, and the Later Zhou granted the title of military governor of the Wuping Jun (seat at Langzhou). From 956 Zhou Xingfeng held Hunan. When Zhou Xingfeng died in 962, his son Zhou Baoquan was young and Zhang Wenbiao rebelled at Hengzhou; the Song army, using the revolt as a pretext, took over Hunan in 963.

吴朝.note: In 938 Ngô Quyền crushed the Southern Han at the Bạch Đằng River, and in 939 he proclaimed himself king, with his capital at Cổ Loa; Vietnamese history calls this the Ngô dynasty. Ngô Quyền died in 944 and Dương Tam Kha usurped the throne; Ngô Xương Ngập and Ngô Xương Văn restored the dynasty. In 965 Ngô Xương Văn was killed in battle, and local strongmen rose everywhere, a period known as the "Rebellion of the Twelve Warlords".

安西.note: The Four Garrisons of Anxi military governorship (Anxi Protectorate), with its seat at Kucha (today's Kuqa), controlling the four garrisons of Kucha, Khotan, Kashgar and Karasahr. In the Tianbao era Gao Xianzhi and then Feng Changqing were military governors; in 747 Gao Xianzhi led a distant expedition against Little Balur. After the An Lushan Rebellion its best troops were moved east, and Guo Xin and others held out alone until the early 9th century, when it fell to Tibet and the Uyghurs.

北庭.note: The Yi–Xi–Beiting military governorship, with its seat at Tingzhou (Beiting Protectorate, the Beiting ruins in today's Jimsar), controlling the region north of the Tian Shan and the two prefectures of Yizhou and Xizhou. After the An Lushan Rebellion it and Anxi depended on each other, keeping in touch with Chang'an by the Uyghur Road; in 790 it fell to Tibet, and the military governor Yang Xigu fled to Xizhou and was later killed by the Uyghurs.

河西.note: The Hexi military governorship, with its seat at Liangzhou, charged with keeping Tibet and the Turks apart; it controlled the Chishui, Dadou, Jiankang, Yumen and Doulu armies, over 70,000 men, and in the Tianbao era Geshu Han held it concurrently. Liangzhou fell in 764 and the military governor moved his seat to Ganzhou and then Shazhou; Ganzhou and Suzhou fell in 766 and Guazhou in 776, and in 786 Shazhou (under Yan Chao) surrendered to Tibet after holding out for more than ten years.

陇右.note: The Longyou military governorship, with its seat at Shanzhou (today's Ledu), defending against Tibet around Qinghai Lake and in Hehuang; it controlled the Lintao, Heyuan, Jishi and other armies, over 70,000 men. In the Tianbao era Geshu Han was its military governor and in 749 stormed Shibao Fortress. After the An Lushan Rebellion its troops were moved east, and in 763 all the prefectures of Longyou fell to Tibet.

朔方.note: The Shuofang military governorship, with its seat at Lingzhou (today's Wuzhong), controlling the three Shouxiang Cities and the Feng'an, Dingyuan and other armies, defending against the Turks and the Uyghurs. In the An Lushan Rebellion Guo Ziyi and Li Guangbi made the Shuofang army the mainstay of the suppression, and in 756 Emperor Suzong took the throne at Lingwu. The fanzhen of Binning, Xiasui, Zhenwu and Tiande were later split off from its territory one by one, and in the late Tang it held only Lingzhou, Yanzhou and a few other prefectures.

关内.note: The Guannei investigation commissioner's circuit (the prefectures of northern Guanzhong where no military governor was established).

京畿.note: The Capital District Circuit, centered on Jingzhao Fu (Chang'an) and directly under the court. At the end of the Tang only Jingzhao, Shangzhou and a few other places remained, and the court's orders did not reach beyond Guanzhong.

河东.note: The Hedong military governorship, with its seat at Taiyuan Fu (the Northern Capital); at the end of the Tianbao era An Lushan held it concurrently. After the rebellion famous generals such as Xin Yunjing, Ma Sui, Wang E and Li Guangyan governed it, and it was the court's key fanzhen for holding Hebei in check. In the 880s Li Keyong of the Shatuo took this fanzhen and contended with Zhu Quanzhong; after 907 it became the state of Jin.

河东道.note: The southern prefectures of the Hedong investigation commissioner's circuit (Puzhou, Jinzhou, Jiangzhou, Zezhou, Luzhou and others), where no military governor was established in the Tianbao era.

范阳.note: The Fanyang military governorship (Youzhou military governorship), with its seat at Youzhou, controlling nine jun, including the Jinglüe, Weiwu and Qingyi Jun, over 90,000 men, to guard against the Xi and the Khitans. From 744 An Lushan held it concurrently, and in 755 he rose in rebellion here. In the 12th month of 757 Shi Siming surrendered to the Tang with Fanyang and twelve other commanderies, and in 758 he rebelled again. After the rebellion it was renamed the Lulong military governorship.

河北道.note: The Hebei investigation commissioner's circuit (Weizhou, Bozhou, Xiangzhou, Weizhou and other prefectures); in the Tianbao era An Lushan was concurrently its investigation commissioner.

平卢.note: The Pinglu military governorship, with its seat at Yingzhou (today's Chaoyang), keeping the Shiwei and the Mohe in check; it controlled the Pinglu and Lulong armies and the Andong Protectorate. An Lushan rose to power here. During the An Lushan Rebellion the Pinglu army commander Hou Xiyi and others stayed loyal to Tang, and in 761 they led 20,000 followers across the sea south to Qingzhou, after which Yingzhou was taken by the Xi and the Khitans.

都畿.note: The Eastern Capital District investigation commissioner's circuit, centered on Henan Fu (the Eastern Capital, Luoyang).

河南道.note: The Henan investigation commissioner's circuit, with its seat at Bianzhou, covering the many prefectures and counties north of the Huai River and south of the Yellow River.

山南东道.note: Seat at Xiangzhou. After the An Lushan Rebellion it was governed in turn by Lai Zhen, Liang Chongyi (who held it 763–781), Yu Di and others; at the end of the Tang Zhao Deyin and his son Zhao Kuangning held it as their own, and in 905 Zhu Quanzhong annexed it.

山南西道.note: Seat at Liangzhou (raised to Xingyuan Fu in 784), guarding the Shu roads across the Qinling Mountains. In 784 Emperor Dezong took refuge here from the rebellions of Zhu Ci and Li Huaiguang. At the end of the Tang Li Maozhen held it; after 903 it passed to Wang Jian's Former Shu.

剑南.note: The Jiannan military governorship, with its seat at Yizhou (raised to Chengdu Fu in 757), resisting Tibet to the west and keeping the Man and Lao tribes in check to the south. In 756 Emperor Xuanzong took refuge in Shu. In 757 it was divided into the two military governorships of Xichuan and Dongchuan.

淮南.note: The Huainan military governorship, with its seat at Yangzhou. Yangzhou was the center of grain transport on the Yangtze and Huai and of overseas trade: "Yangzhou first, Yizhou second." After the An Lushan Rebellion Gao Shi, Chen Shaoyou, Du You, Li Jifu, Li Deyu, Gao Pian and others governed it in turn; in 887 Gao Pian was killed by his own officers and Yangzhou was laid waste. Yang Xingmi took the region in 892 and was invested as Prince of Wu in 902.

江南东道.note: The investigation commissioner of the Jiangnan East Circuit (seat at Suzhou), covering today's southern Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Fujian.

江南西道.note: The investigation commissioner of the Jiangnan West Circuit (seat at Hongzhou), covering today's southern Anhui, Jiangxi, Hunan and southeastern Hubei.

黔中.note: The Qianzhong investigation commissioner and Qianzhou surveillance commissioner, with the seat at Qianzhou (today's Pengshui, Chongqing), controlling many loose-rein tribal prefectures in today's northeastern Guizhou, western Hunan and southeastern Chongqing.

岭南.note: The Lingnan pacification commissioner of the Five Commands (Tianbao era), with the seat at Guangzhou, controlling the Five Commands of Guang, Gui, Rong, Yong and Annan. After the rebellion it was divided into the Lingnan East Circuit (Guangzhou) and the Gui, Rong, Yong and Annan commands. Guangzhou was the greatest port of overseas trade, with a maritime trade commissioner. At the end of the Tang Liu Yin held the region, and in 917 his younger brother Liu Yan proclaimed himself emperor (Southern Han).

卢龙.note: Fanyang renamed, with its seat at Youzhou. In 763 the surrendered rebel general Li Huaixian was appointed military governor; after him Zhu Xicai, Zhu Ci, Zhu Tao, Liu Peng–Liu Ji–Liu Zong, Zhang Zhongwu, Zhang Yunshen and others set themselves up in turn. One of the three Hebei fanzhen, it saw repeated mutinies. In 895 Li Keyong installed Liu Rengong here; the Liu family soon turned against Jin and went its own way, and after 907 it became Yan.

成德.note: Seat at Hengzhou (renamed Zhenzhou in 820 to avoid the personal name of Emperor Muzong; today's Zhengding). The surrendered rebel general Li Baochen (Zhang Zhongzhi) first held it; two lines, Wang Wujun–Wang Shizhen–Wang Chengzong and Wang Tingcou–Wang Yuankui–Wang Rong, then held it by inheritance; in all, Chengde was autonomous for nearly 160 years. It was one of the three Hebei fanzhen. After 907 Wang Rong styled himself Prince of Zhao; in 921 he was killed by his officer Zhang Wenli, and in 922 the fanzhen passed to Jin.

魏博.note: Seat at Weizhou. The surrendered rebel general Tian Chengsi first held it, followed in turn by the Tian, Shi, He, Han, Yue and Luo families. Its headquarters troops were arrogant and unruly: "In Chang'an, the Son of Heaven; in Weizhou, the headquarters troops." It was the strongest of the three Hebei fanzhen. From 812 to 820, under Tian Hongzheng, Weibo was loyal to the court. In 906 Luo Shaowei borrowed Zhu Quanzhong's troops and wiped out the 8,000 households of the headquarters troops, after which Weibo declined.

相卫.note: Held by the surrendered rebel general Xue Song, with its seat at Xiangzhou, and known at the time as the Zhaoyi Jun. Xue Song died in 773, and in 775 Tian Chengsi seized the prefectures of Xiangwei, which brought a punitive campaign from the court.

淄青.note: The Pinglu–Ziqing military governorship, with its seat at Qingzhou (moved to Yunzhou in 776). In 761 the Pinglu army crossed the sea southward; in 765 Li Zhengji drove out Hou Xiyi and set himself up, and in 776 he expanded to fifteen prefectures. Li Zhengji, Li Na, Li Shigu and Li Shidao held it in four successions for over fifty years, controlling the profits of salt and iron and repeatedly sending assassins. In 819 Emperor Xianzong put down Li Shidao and divided the fanzhen into the three fanzhen of Tianping, Pinglu and Yanhai.

汴宋.note: The Henan military governorship, with its seat at Bianzhou, commanding grain transport on the Bian River. Tian Shengong and Li Lingyao held it in turn; in 776 Li Lingyao rebelled and was put down, and his prefectures were divided up by Li Zhengji and others.

滑亳.note: The Huabo military governorship (Linghu Zhang), with its seat at Huazhou, later renamed the Yongping Jun and then the Yicheng Jun.

泽潞.note: The Zelu military governorship (the brothers Li Baoyu and Li Baozhen), with its seat at Luzhou. In the 780s it was merged with Xiangwei into the Zhaoyi Jun.

东都畿.note: The chief defense commissioner of the Eastern Capital District and Ruzhou, and the custodian of the Eastern Capital, with the seat at Henan Fu (Luoyang).

陕虢.note: The Shanguo surveillance commissioner (Baoyi Jun), with the seat at Shanzhou, guarding the Sanmen Gorge on the grain-transport route east of Tong Pass.

河中.note: The Hezhong military governorship (Huguo Jun), with its seat at Hezhong Fu (Puzhou), commanding the Pujin Ford and linking Guanzhong with Hedong. At the end of the Tang Wang Chongrong, Wang Chongying and Wang Ke held it in turn and married into Li Keyong's family; in 901 Zhu Quanzhong annexed it.

鄜坊.note: The Fu–Fang–Dan–Yan military governorship (Baoda Jun), with its seat at Fuzhou, screening Chang'an to the north.

凤翔.note: The Fengxiang military governorship, with its seat at Fengxiang Fu (Qizhou), the western gateway to Chang'an; in 757 Emperor Suzong made it his temporary capital. At the end of the Tang Li Maozhen held it; it became the later state of Qi.

荆南.note: The Jingnan military governorship, with its seat at Jiangling Fu, a key fanzhen on the middle Yangtze and a hub of north–south transport by water and land. At the end of the Tang Cheng Rui held it (888–903); in 907 Gao Jichang took charge of it on the orders of Liang, and it became the later state of Jingnan (Nanping).

西川.note: The Jiannan Xichuan military governorship, with its seat at Chengdu Fu, defending against Tibet and Nanzhao. Wei Gao governed Shu for twenty-one years (785–805) and allied with Nanzhao to defeat Tibet; in 806 Liu Pi rebelled and was put down. In 829 and in 869–870 Nanzhao armies twice reached Chengdu. Wang Jian entered Chengdu in 891 and proclaimed himself emperor in 907 (Former Shu).

东川.note: The Jiannan Dongchuan military governorship, with its seat at Zizhou (today's Santai). At the end of the Tang the brothers Gu Yanlang and Gu Yanhui held it; in 897 Wang Jian annexed it.

淮西.note: The Huaixi military governorship (Zhangyi Jun), with its seat at Caizhou. Li Zhongchen, Li Xilie, Chen Xianqi, Wu Shaocheng, Wu Shaoyang and Wu Yuanji held it in turn as their own for over thirty years, astride the grain route of the Yangtze and Huai. In the 10th month of 817 Li Su made a surprise attack on Caizhou on a snowy night and captured Wu Yuanji; Huaixi was pacified and its prefectures were divided among the neighboring fanzhen.

鄂岳.note: The Eyue surveillance commissioner (Wuchang Jun), with the seat at Ezhou. At the end of the Tang Du Hong held it; in 905 Yang Xingmi annexed it.

浙西.note: The surveillance commissioner of the Zhejiang West Circuit (Zhenhai Jun), with the seat at Runzhou; one of the most important sources of revenue for the late Tang. In 807 Li Qi rebelled and was put down. At the end of the Tang Qian Liu became military governor of the Zhenhai Jun and moved the seat to Hangzhou.

浙东.note: The surveillance commissioner of the Zhejiang East Circuit (Yisheng Jun), with the seat at Yuezhou. Qiu Fu's rising took place here in 859–860. At the end of the Tang Dong Chang held it and proclaimed himself emperor in 895.

宣歙.note: The Xuanshe surveillance commissioner (Ningguo Jun), with the seat at Xuanzhou. Yang Xingmi took Xuanzhou in 889 and made it his base.

江西.note: The surveillance commissioner of the Jiangnan West Circuit (Zhennan Jun), with the seat at Hongzhou. At the end of the Tang Zhong Chuan held Hongzhou (882–906); after his death it was annexed by the Yang family's Wu.

湖南.note: The Hunan surveillance commissioner (Wu'an Jun), with the seat at Tanzhou. In 894 Liu Jianfeng and Ma Yin, leading the remnants of Sun Ru's army, entered Tanzhou; in 896 Ma Yin succeeded, and it became the later state of Chu.

福建.note: The Fujian surveillance commissioner (Weiwu Jun), with the seat at Fuzhou. In 893 Wang Chao and Wang Shenzhi took Fuzhou; after 907 it became the state of Min.

桂管.note: The Gui Command pacification commissioner (Jingjiang Jun), with the seat at Guizhou. In 868 Pang Xun and other soldiers from Xuzhou garrisoning Guizhou mutinied and marched north, setting off the Pang Xun rebellion. After 900 it was taken by the Ma family's Chu.

容管.note: The Rong Command pacification commissioner (Ningyuan Jun), with the seat at Rongzhou. At the end of the Tang Pang Juzhao held it; in 911 he surrendered to Southern Han.

邕管.note: The Yong Command pacification commissioner (Jianwu Jun), with the seat at Yongzhou, defending against the Xiyuan tribes and Nanzhao. At the end of the Tang Ye Guanglüe held it; in 911 Southern Han annexed it.

安南.note: The Annan Protectorate (renamed the Jinghai Jun in 866), with its seat at Giao Châu (Tống Bình, today's Hanoi). Between 858 and 866 Nanzhao took it several times; in 866 Gao Pian recovered it and built the city of Đại La. In 905 the local magnate Khúc Thừa Dụ proclaimed himself military governor, opening a period of self-rule; Dương Đình Nghệ in 931 and Ngô Quyền in 938 drove out Southern Han armies in turn. In 968 Đinh Bộ Lĩnh founded the state of Đại Cồ Việt, and Vietnam became independent.

昭义.note: The Zhaoyi Jun (Zelu), with its seat at Luzhou, also holding the three prefectures of Xingzhou, Mingzhou and Cizhou east of the Taihang Mountains; it was the court's wedge driven between the three Hebei fanzhen. In 843 Liu Zhen defied the court, and in 844 a campaign directed by Li Deyu put him down. At the end of the Tang Li Keyong held it, while Xing, Ming and Ci were taken by Zhu Quanzhong.

宣武.note: The Xuanwu Jun, with its seat at Bianzhou (at first at Songzhou), holding the choke point of grain transport on the Bian River and notorious for its arrogant troops. In 883 Zhu Quanzhong (Zhu Wen) became military governor of Xuanwu; from this base he swallowed up the fanzhen of Henan, and in 907 he usurped the Tang throne.

义成.note: The Yicheng Jun, with its seat at Huazhou, guarding the Baima Ford on the Yellow River.

义武.note: The Yiwu Jun, split off from Chengde in 782, with its seat at Dingzhou; Zhang Xiaozhong was its first military governor. In 810 Zhang Maozhao went to court with his whole clan. At the end of the Tang Wang Chucun, Wang Gao and Wang Chuzhi held it in turn, and after 907 Wang Chuzhi styled himself Prince of Beiping; in 921 Wang Du imprisoned his father and took over, and in 929 Later Tang put him down.

邠宁.note: The Binning military governorship (Jingnan Jun), with its seat at Binzhou, screening Chang'an to the northwest. In 895 its military governor Wang Xingyu marched on the capital with Li Maozhen and Han Jian, and was put down and killed by Li Keyong.

横海.note: The Henghai Jun (Cang–Jing), split off from Yiwu in 785, with its seat at Cangzhou; Cheng Rihua, Cheng Huaizhi and others held it by inheritance. At the end of the Tang it was renamed the Yichang Jun, and in 898 Liu Rengong annexed it.

武宁.note: The Wuning Jun, with its seat at Xuzhou, guarding the southern stretch of the Bian River and the region north of the Huai, and notorious for unruly units such as the Silver Sabre Corps. The Pang Xun rebellion of 868–869 centered on Xuzhou. At the end of the Tang Shi Pu held it; in 893 Zhu Quanzhong destroyed him.

忠武.note: The Zhongwu Jun (Chen–Xu), with its seat at Xuzhou; the troops of Chen and Xu were famed as fighters and did much in the campaign to pacify Huaixi.

河阳.note: The Three Cities of Heyang military governorship, guarding the Mengjin Ford on the Yellow River and protecting the Eastern Capital; Mengzhou was established in 843.

泾原.note: The Jingyuan military governorship, with its seat at Jingzhou, established in 768 on the front line against Tibet. In 783 the Jingyuan troops mutinied while passing through Chang'an and raised Zhu Ci to power.

夏绥.note: The Xia–Sui–Yin–You military governorship, with its seat at Xiazhou (Tongwan City), defending against the Tanguts and Tibet. In 881 Tuoba Sigong of the Tanguts became military governor, and it was soon renamed the Dingnan Jun.

振武.note: The Zhenwu Jun, with its seat at the Chanyu Protectorate (today's Horinger), defending against the Uyghurs, the Shatuo and the Tatars. In 843 Liu Mian and Shi Xiong marched out from here and crushed the Uyghur Wujie Khagan at Mount Shahu.

天德.note: The Tiande Jun, with its seat around the Western Shouxiang City (later moved to the old Tiande city), screening the Ordos Loop; it was the gateway for traffic between Tang and the Uyghurs.

天平.note: Created in 819 from part of Ziqing, with its seat at Yunzhou. At the end of the Tang Zhu Xuan held it; in 897 Zhu Quanzhong destroyed him.

平卢·青.note: The Pinglu Jun after the division of Ziqing in 819, with its seat at Qingzhou, holding the five prefectures of Qingzhou, Zizhou, Qizhou, Dengzhou and Laizhou. At the end of the Tang Wang Shifan held it; in 903 he surrendered to Zhu Quanzhong.

泰宁.note: Created in 819 from part of Ziqing as the Yanhai surveillance commissioner, later raised to the Taining Jun, with its seat at Yanzhou. At the end of the Tang Zhu Jin held it; in 897 Zhu Quanzhong seized it, and Zhu Jin fled to Yang Xingmi in Huainan.

秦成.note: Established after Qinzhou was recovered in 849, with its seat at Qinzhou, defending against the Tibetan tribes; it later became the Tianxiong Jun military governorship.

奉国.note: Qin Zongquan of Caizhou was appointed defense commissioner of the Fengguo Jun in 881. In 883 he surrendered to Huang Chao; after Huang Chao's death he proclaimed himself emperor and massacred and plundered in all directions. In 888 his officer Shen Cong seized him and handed him over to Zhu Quanzhong; he was beheaded at Chang'an in 889.

大同.note: The Datong Jun defense commissioner, with the seat at Yunzhou, controlling Yunzhou, Yuzhou, Shuozhou and other prefectures; Li Guochang and his son Li Keyong of the Shatuo once rose here (878).

镇国.note: The Zhenguo Jun, with its seat at Huazhou, guarding Tong Pass. At the end of the Tang Han Jian held it, and in 896–898 Emperor Zhaozong was forced to live at Huazhou.

镇海.note: At the end of the Tang Qian Liu, as military governor of the Zhenhai Jun, held Hangzhou and southern Zhexi. In 896 he destroyed Dong Chang and held both Zhexi and Zhedong; after 907 it became the state of Wuyue.

危全讽.note: Wei Quanfeng held Fuzhou and his younger brother Wei Zichang held Xinzhou (c. 882–909); in 909 the Yang family's Wu defeated them at the Battle of Xiangyatan.

虔州.note: Lu Guangchou took Qianzhou in 885 and later Shaozhou, wavering between Liang, Wu and Southern Han; in 918 Qianzhou was taken by Wu.

武贞.note: Lei Man took Langzhou in 881 and was an enemy of Cheng Rui of Jingnan; in 908 his son Lei Yangong was overthrown by Chu.

西川·孟.note: After Later Tang destroyed Former Shu, Meng Zhixiang was made military governor of Xichuan in 925. From 930 he joined Dong Zhang of Dongchuan in defying the court; in 932 he annexed Dongchuan, and in 934 he proclaimed himself emperor and founded Later Shu.

东川·董.note: In 925 Later Tang made Dong Zhang military governor of Dongchuan. In 930 he and Meng Zhixiang together defied the court; in 932 the two Chuan turned on each other, and Dong Zhang was defeated and died.

深赵.note: In 782 the court split Chengde into three fanzhen and made Kang Rizhi military training and surveillance commissioner of Shenzhao, with his seat at Zhaozhou. Shenzhou was soon seized by Zhu Tao, leaving Kang Rizhi only Zhaozhou; after Wang Wujun submitted in 784, Shenzhou and Zhaozhou went back to Chengde.

庞勋.note: In the 7th month of 868, eight hundred Xuzhou soldiers garrisoning Guizhou, whose tour of duty had been extended again and again, killed their commander and marched home north under the grain-and-fodder clerk Pang Xun. Sweeping up followers along the way, they took Xuzhou in the 10th month and held Xuzhou, Suzhou, Haozhou and other prefectures, with as many as 200,000 men, cutting the Jiang–Huai canal route. The court made Kang Chengxun military governor of Yicheng and commander-in-chief of the Xu–Si field army and, with troops borrowed from the Shatuo leader Zhuye Chixin, crushed the rising; in the 9th month of 869 Pang Xun was killed in battle at Qi County. After the campaign Zhuye Chixin was given the name Li Guochang, and the power of the Shatuo began to rise.
